name: LEXICON
expansion: Lexical Encoding of eXperiment Information as Checked Observable tokeNs

intro.problem: Detector events are treated as vectors of continuous features, and the co-occurrence tools that let language models learn structure [@levy2014] have barely been tried on them; the closest precedent tokenizes whole events for anomaly detection [@visive2025]. Co-occurrence alone gives a density, not a grammar; the open question is whether hidden structure lies behind it.
intro.value: A token model trained only on background could score how typical an event is, giving a new axis for a data-driven background estimate; token embeddings could become classifier inputs, as tokenized jets already have [@finke2023][@birk2024]; and hidden structure that matches the decay chain would show what the networks are learning.
intro.approach: Each feature is quantized with evidence-based edges [@scargle2013], so an event becomes a set of tokens. Density models, scored by exact likelihood where possible, measure how much the tokens share beyond independence [@watanabe1960]; latent models ask what form it takes. Signal and background are compared by likelihood ratio [@neyman1933], dependency trees [@chowliu1968] and a pre-registered decay chain.
intro.goals: Three verdicts, kept separate: whether background tokens have stable hidden structure, whether signal's structure differs from background's, and whether a token score makes a better ABCD axis. Each token axis is built only from the features of the network it replaces, and confirmation runs follow rules frozen before they start.

questions: Does co-occurrence among binned detector features carry signal-versus-background information beyond the raw values?
Is there hidden structure behind background co-occurrence: how much, and in what form, whether token classes, event types, a hierarchy or a feature order?
Does signal's structure differ from background's, in its relations, its order or the decay chain that produced it, beyond what single tokens carry?

tagline: Detector events as tokens: does an event have a grammar?

components.name: Route A1
components.subtitle: Background-only surprise as an ABCD axis
components.summary: Token models trained on background alone (this was Route A before the split) score how surprising each event is, and that score replaces one network as an axis of the ABCD plane. Signal labels and network scores never enter the token models, and each model sees only the features of the network it replaces, so the axis can be independent of the other. Two such models, one per network, also give a plane with no labels on either axis. The same background models measure how much the tokens share beyond independence; what form that takes is left to the latent models.

items.label: Independence
items.detail: Product of per-feature marginals: the floor every other model must beat

items.label: Pairs and triples
items.detail: Count models over feature pairs and triples; the best model in the data-starved barrel

items.label: Grammar budget
items.detail: Total correlation, the information by which tokens fall short of independence, and the share of it a tree, pairs and triples each capture [@watanabe1960][@chowliu1968]

items.label: CutFormer
items.detail: Masked-token transformer with feature-ID embeddings and no positions [@golling2024][@vaswani2017]; the best model in the endcap

items.label: Evt2Vec
items.detail: Skip-gram token embeddings [@levy2014] as a comparison

items.label: Attention test
items.detail: The same transformer with its attention fixed to uniform, so it can mix context but not choose it [@zaheer2017]; separates what attention selects from what extra capacity buys

components.name: Route A1 variant
components.subtitle: Exact likelihood
components.summary: The transformer's pseudo-likelihood is not a normalized density and undercounts redundant features that predict each other. An autoregressive model gives an exact negative log-likelihood by the chain rule, which holds for any feature order, so the ordering that rules recurrence out of a classifier is legitimate for a density. Orders are averaged as a nuisance, but each order's held-out likelihood is kept, so whether some orders fit better than others is measured rather than assumed. Status: the variants and a pre-registered evaluation are written down and under review; nothing has run yet. Runs start in the barrel, and only variants that pass there go on to the endcap.

items.label: Exact count models
items.detail: Tree and small-graph models of pair counts: an exact likelihood with no training seed

items.label: MADE
items.detail: Masked autoregressive MLP [@germain2015]; set aside for a model that shares weights across orders, kept as a control, and fitted separately on a few fixed orders as the clean test of whether any order fits better

items.label: Any-order CutFormer
items.detail: Same transformer trained over random orders, giving an exact likelihood averaged across them; compared on equal terms with the masked MLP and the recurrent model

items.label: GRU
items.detail: Background-only recurrent density over a fixed feature order [@cho2014], within one network's features; kept because barrel runs are cheap, always read beside the other exact models

items.label: Order ensemble
items.detail: Several random orderings averaged, with their spread as a per-event uncertainty [@uria2014]; each order's held-out likelihood is also logged and compared with seed-to-seed scatter

items.label: Order search
items.detail: Greedy orders built from the any-order model's conditionals, one feature at a time, after a search over orders [@teyssier2005]; proposed on one set of folds and scored on another

items.label: Gates
items.detail: Per-feature sigmoid gates showing which features carry the surprise; deferred

components.name: Latent grammar
components.subtitle: Hidden structure behind the co-occurrence; background first
components.summary: Density models show how much structure the tokens share, not what it is. Latent models look for its form: token classes, event types or factors that, once known, leave the tokens nearly independent. Every model, latent or not, is scored on one card. A latent model counts as structure only if it fits held-out background, explains the shared information and stays stable across seeds, folds and tokenizations; it is called a grammar only if that structure is hierarchical or follows the decay chain. Background comes first; signal enters after the token audit.

items.label: Token classes
items.detail: Tokens grouped into classes that keep most of the pairwise information, as in class-based language models [@brown1992]

items.label: Event types
items.detail: A latent class model: events drawn from a few production regimes, tokens independent within each

items.label: Correlation explanation
items.detail: Latent factors ranked by how much of the total correlation each explains, stacked into a hierarchy [@versteeg2014][@versteeg2015]

items.label: One scorecard
items.detail: Held-out exact fit, share of the shared information explained, compression, stability, signal contrast and agreement with the decay chain, for every model; scores a model cannot produce are marked, never converted

items.label: Gates
items.detail: Fit, then explanation measured on held-out events rather than taken from the model, then stability [@vinh2010]; signal contrast and agreement with the decay chain are read only after all three pass

components.name: Route A2
components.subtitle: Signal token models
components.summary: Fit the same token models to signal, read through the edges fitted on background so both use one vocabulary and no label enters the tokenizer. Asks whether signal has a structure of its own, whether it holds across the signal hypotheses, and where signal sits among background's tokens. It uses labels, so it is not background-only, and its tokens are audited for simulation-versus-data artifacts before anything is claimed.

items.label: Same ladder
items.detail: Independence, pair and triple counts, a tree model with an exact likelihood [@chowliu1968], and the transformer where signal statistics allow

items.label: Signal statistics
items.detail: Few signal events per hypothesis: pool them with the hypothesis as a conditioning token, or fine-tune from the background model

items.label: Occupancy
items.detail: Where signal lands in background's vocabulary; the tokens it fills that background rarely does become the audit list

items.label: Signal transformer
items.detail: Fine-tuned from the background transformer where signal allows; it must beat the tree model and the uniform-attention control on held-out signal

items.label: Signal structure
items.detail: Tree skeletons fitted to signal and to background separately and compared edge by edge, with bootstrap stability and a small-sample correction to the mutual information [@chowliu1968][@paninski2003]

components.name: Route A3
components.subtitle: Signal against background
components.summary: Compare the signal and background models. Their log-likelihood ratio is the optimal discriminant when the densities are right [@neyman1933]; for tree models it splits exactly into a marginal term, what each token carries alone, and a relational term, what the relations between tokens carry. Whether the relational term adds separation is the most direct test of whether events have a grammar. The same comparison shows where the networks' information comes from and which relations cross the split between the two networks.

items.label: Grammar contrast
items.detail: Pair by pair, how much more or less two tokens co-occur in signal than in background, with a false-discovery control and replication on new folds

items.label: Exact decomposition
items.detail: Marginal plus relational terms on a tree skeleton chosen from background alone [@chowliu1968]

items.label: Structure contrast
items.detail: The same ratio with each class on its own tree; the gap from the shared-skeleton ratio is what a change of structure carries, beyond a change of strength

items.label: Order against physics
items.detail: Expected orderings from detector geometry and the decay chain are written down before any order is learned; data alone fix an order only up to equivalent structures [@verma1990]

items.label: Chain test
items.detail: A decay chain is a Markov chain: given the middle step, its two ends share little information. Conditional mutual information along the chain written down in advance, compared between signal and background with a within-stratum permutation null [@cover2006]

items.label: Ratio as an axis
items.detail: Built per network feature set and tested for closure like any network score; it is supervised, not background-only

items.label: Transformer ratios
items.detail: Approximate and exact transformer likelihood ratios, read against the exact tree ratio rather than trusted on their own

components.name: Route B
components.subtitle: Supervised on tokens
components.summary: Use the labels with discriminative models on tokens: a linear read-out of the tokens, a probe on the background model's embeddings, a fine-tuned transformer, and embeddings into a small network. The generative form, a likelihood ratio between signal and background token densities, is now Route A3.

items.label: Audit first
items.detail: Check tokens that appear only in signal for simulation-versus-data artifacts before trusting them

items.label: Attention pooling
items.detail: A learned query attends over the token states to build one vector per event [@lee2019], tested against plain averaging

items.label: Attention is not an explanation
items.detail: Attention maps are a cross-check against the count and tree structure, not evidence of a grammar [@jain2019][@wiegreffe2019]

items.label: No recurrent classifier
items.detail: A recurrent network imposes a fixed order the features are not given; as a density that is harmless, as a classifier it is not, so it is not used here

components.name: Route C
components.subtitle: Tokens into the networks
components.summary: Feed token or event embeddings to the existing networks as inputs; per-event pooled vectors are where the value is expected to be. Attention stays within one network's inputs and never runs across the two networks' feature sets.

results.title: First comparisons are a baseline
results.text: Summed surprise was first built from every feature, so it shared inputs with the network it was paired with. In the barrel it closed often but carried little signal; in the endcap it came about as close to closure as the regularized network pairs while keeping less signal in the signal region. Because of the shared inputs, neither result is a fair test; both are being rerun with separated features.

results.title: Background tokens predict each other
results.text: Co-occurrence structure is real and large in both regions, mostly through pairs. In the barrel, simple pair-and-triple counts beat the transformer on every seed; in the endcap, the larger sample lets the transformer go further.

results.title: Tokenizing is cheap
results.text: Coarse binning in the barrel loses only a small share of the raw-value context information; finer bins starve for events.

results.title: Signal information cancels in the sum
results.text: Individual tokens carry signal information in both directions, so summing surprise over features cancels it, which is why total surprise is a weak classifier.

results.title: Bin edges matter in the tail
results.text: An open top quantile bin hides the signal tail; evidence-based edges split it and move signal onto rare tokens [@scargle2013].

results.title: Not yet a measurement
results.text: Comparisons are single-seed, use the wide first-round network sweep rather than the refined models, and pick the surprise sign after seeing data; the separated-feature runs come first, then multiple seeds.

open.text: A recurrent model (GRU) is used only as a density: the chain rule holds for any feature order, so an exact likelihood is legitimate, but as a classifier it would impose a fixed order the features are not given. Whether a learned order exists is now a question to measure, not an assumption either way. It appears in Routes A1, A2 and A3 as a density or a ratio of densities, with several random orders averaged, and not in Route B or as a network input encoder.

Transformers already sit at the center of the token models, but nothing yet shows that their attention, rather than their size, does the work. Every attention claim is now read against the same model with attention fixed to uniform, and against simple counts; that test comes before any new transformer variant.

Grammar on this page has two parts. Its amount is the information tokens share beyond independence, which every density model measures. Its form is hidden structure that leaves the tokens nearly independent once known, which only the latent models can show. A model that measures the amount without passing the latent gates is a density, not a grammar.
The count models report a pseudo-likelihood, which cannot be ranked against exact models; they need exact versions before the scorecard can include them.

Order is so far learned over the observed features, and the decay chain is only tested where it is written down in advance. Whether a sequence can be found among the latent factors themselves is not yet planned.
